text.p: A slew of domestic economic data will help give direction to Australian markets this week, with most traders looking to retail trade and building approvals data to confirm expectations of economic revival.
December quarter gross domestic product data, due out Wednesday, will give also give a fix on the strength of the economy in late 1996, while the Reserve Bank board meets on Tuesday.
"We expect a solid two percent rebound in retail sales in January after a sedate December quarter," said Westpac Banking Corp in a market note.
"Such a result would confirm our view that, with the economy becoming increasingly stronger in recent months, the RBA wil hold its current policy line for the foreseeable future."

Building approvals are also seen rising from historically low levels. "Home building has been in the doldrums for two years and any increase in activity would be welcome," said Colonial State bank, which expects a rise of 2.5 percent.
World markets will await the second leg of U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey Hawkins testimony on March 5, after his comments last week sparked a sell-off in U.S. Treasuries.
Key U.S. data due for release includes the February NAPM on Monday and February non-farm payroll employment figures on Friday.

"Given the recent Greenspan comments, any signs of furtehr strength in these numbers is likely to further spook U.S. credit markets that the Fed may be in tightening mode again the in the not too distant future," said Westpac.
In the stock market, Boral Ltd, Amcor Ltd and Southcorp Holdings Ltd report this week, as do Woodside Petroleum Ltd and AGL among resource stocks.
BONDS (Fri 10-yr cash yield 7.70 pct, 3-yr 6.91 pct)
The Australian bond market faces another volatile week with a wealth of data due for release locally and several key events in the U.S. which will grip markets worldwide.

Wednesday's second leg of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony is likely to hold centre stage overall, particularly in the light of his comments last week when he said he could not rule out a pre-emptive tightening in U.S. monetary policy.
Local long-dated yields rose to their highest level for the year in tandem with U.S. treasuries on Greenspan's first thoughts on the current state of the U.S. economy.
However, moderate outcomes in wages data for both enterprise bargaining agreements and average weekly earnings helped to stem some of the negative sentiment from the U.S..
This Friday also sees the all important monthly U.S. non-farm payrolls report, which has long been seen as the barometer for the Fed's thinking on policy.

Locally sees an unusual stream of data, including third quarter GDP on Wednesday, but the main focus for bonds could be on Tuesday's retail trade and building approvals reports, given that they are more up to date indicators for January.
"Against the bearish U.S. backdrop, the outlook for Australian bonds is not good," said economists at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"The risk on next week's data, running from the stocks data to the retail sales and the building approvals, is for stronger than expected outcomes," they added.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri 0.7750/55, New York 0.7756/61)
The Australian dollar starts in consolidation mode after surviving sustained profit taking last week and having surged more than two cents from a one year low of US$0.7550 in just a fortnight.
The initial guiding should be US$0.7735 support and US$0.7820 resistance and analysts leaned toward an eventual break of the latter, while emphasising the call was touch and go.

Much, for instance, depended on whether Japanese investors continued to repatriate funds at the rate of recent days which had seen a host of currencies lose ground as short yen positions were closed out.
Dealers said a range of Japanese companies and institutions were realising profits on offshore assets with the aim of padding balance sheets ahead of their March 31 financial year.
That trend had dragged the dollar off to 93.21/31 by Friday from 95.16/26 a week before.

Most expected the Japanese funds to return once the year-end was past since the Australian currency still offered a hefty interest rate premium to the yen and the risk of another policy easing here had faded in the face of upbeat domestic data.
Of this week's smorgasbord of figures analysts reckoned the quarterly numbers were largely of historical interest, and that included the GDP report.
Perhaps more important would be January retail sales and building approvals which would indicate how consumer demand and the housing market was responding to the last rate cut on December 11.

The RBA has already said it detected a pick-up in activity such that current policy settings were appropriate for the time being. Any weakness in these figures, therefore, would be disappointing for the dollar as well as the bank.
ECONOMIC DATA
A hectic week for Australian markets begins on Monday with the release of two sets of data, one out for the first time and the other seen as a key contributor to fourth quarter GDP forecasts.
The balance of goods and services report will make its debut for the month of January, replacing the monthly current account deficit.
Forecasts for the new series range widely but the strength of imports in January, coupled with a belief that exports will not match their December strength, means it should open with a deficit.

Also out Monday, business inventories are expected to have risen in the December quarter, but will make a negative contribution to GDP. This is because the rate of increase in December quarter stocks will be slower than in the September quarter, leading to a negative overall contribution.
Stocks are very hard to forcecast, and can fall well outside expectations. For that reason, they are regarded as important for finalising GDP forecasts.
On Tuesday, January retail trade and building approvals and December quarter balance of payments data are released.

Retail trade is one of the more important figures of the week, with economists looking for confirmation of anecdotal evidence of improved trading conditions and expectations of stronger growth in 1997.
The Reserve Bank of Australia Board also meets on Tuesday, in probably the least anticipated meeting since last the one at the beginning of last July.

Recent RBA comments and stronger data have reduced expectations of another easing. Many commentators believe the easing cycle has come to an end, and that the next move in interest rates will be up, in either late 1997 or early 1998.

December quarter GDP is due out Wednesday, but the historical nature of the data and the paring back of rate cut expectations means the data will have a limited impact on markets unless well away from expectations.

December quarter foreign debt, due Thursday, is the least awaited piece of data for the week. The exchange rate ended the year virtually unchanged from its end-September level. The net debt level should rise slightly, reflecting the financing of the ongoing current account deficit.
AUSTRALIAN EQUITIES (Fri All Ords 2,449.90, -14.8)
Equity markets, are getting to the latter stages of the half-year earnings reporting period, with companies recording mixed to slightly better than expected results.

The Australian share market is likely to consolidate around current levels after falling one percent this week, with most of the falls coming on Thursday and Friday as investors worried over U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's comments.

"I think overseas markets will still have a major influence as we will have to see if they re-evaluate Greenspan's comments the way we have done," said Rodney Green chief investment officer at Perpetual Funds Management.

Green said the market has not been too affected by the current earnings period as they are largely within expectations. "These profits are coming out to or above expectation, so no real negatives surprises there. We all know the economy is on the mend so profits will improve," Green said.
Traders will take a keen interest in industrial group's Boral Ltd, Amcor Ltd and Southcorp Holdings Ltd for signs of an improving trading environment.
Woodside Petroleum Ltd and AGL are the main resource groups to report next week.
